tells.1: The generic transition “The consequences are significant” adds emphasis without information and makes the structure feel templated.
tells.2: The accumulation of casual phrases—“sit uncovered,” “actually accept,” “bunch up,” “in the loop”—feels like a deliberate conversational rewrite rather than a natural PRD voice.
tells.4: “This causes four problems” unnecessarily announces the list’s length, giving otherwise straightforward prose a mechanical feel.
tells.5: “What this costs” feels like an inserted punchy heading, particularly because the list includes variability in outcomes rather than just costs.

reason: Version 3 has the most natural balance of direct prose, readable structure, and professional tone; these stylistic judgments do not establish authorship. Before sending, I would fix the substantive issue shared by all five: escalation does not mean a visit has been rescheduled.
